questions.question: Explain the difference between var, let, and const in terms of scope, hoisting, and the temporal dead zone.
questions.answer:
var: function-scoped (or global if top-level). Hoisted and initialised to undefined. Can be re-declared. No TDZ.

let: block-scoped. Hoisted but NOT initialised — accessing before declaration throws a ReferenceError (Temporal Dead Zone). Cannot be re-declared in same scope.

const: same as let for scope and TDZ, but the binding cannot be reassigned after initialisation. The value itself can still be mutated (e.g. pushing to a const array).
questions.tip: Always mention that const gives you an immutable BINDING, not an immutable VALUE. This trips up many candidates.
followUps: Why was let/const introduced if var existed?
What is the TDZ (Temporal Dead Zone) internally?

questions.question: Why does let create a new binding per loop iteration but var doesn't? What does the spec say?
questions.answer:
The ECMAScript spec says that for for loops with let, a new lexical environment is created for each iteration — so each closure gets its own copy of the iteration variable. The engine also copies the variable's value from the previous iteration into the new environment.

For var, there is no per-iteration scope — all iterations share one binding in the containing function scope. Closures capture a reference to this single binding.
questions.tip: Referencing the ECMAScript spec (section 14.7.4) in an interview immediately signals deep preparation.
followUps: Does for...of also create a new binding per iteration?

questions.question: Is it ever correct to use var in modern JavaScript? Give a real scenario.
questions.answer:
In practice, almost never — but there are edge cases:

1. Global intentional declarations: var at the top level adds a property to the window object, which some legacy code relies on.

2. Function-scoped flag patterns: Rare cases where you explicitly want a variable to persist beyond a block inside a function.

3. Legacy code maintenance: Mixing var and let in the same codebase can introduce subtle bugs — sometimes consistency in old code is safer.

In modern code, prefer const by default, let when reassignment is needed, and never var.
questions.tip: This question tests judgment, not just knowledge. Show you understand WHY the rule exists, not just that the rule exists.
followUps: Does strict mode affect var behaviour?

questions.title: var ignores block scope
questions.explanation:
Output: "inner"
Both var declarations refer to the same variable because var ignores block scope. The second var x = 'inner' simply reassigns the same x. If this were let, the inner x would be a separate block-scoped variable and outer x would remain "outer".

questions.title: Closure captures var — tricky timing
questions.explanation:
Output: 3 3 3
All arrow functions share the SAME i (var is function-scoped). The loop runs to completion (i = 3) before any function is ever called. Every closure reads i = 3 at call time.
questions.concept: All closures share one var binding

questions.title: let per-iteration binding
questions.explanation:
Output: 0 1 2
let creates a fresh binding for each iteration. Each closure captures its own i. This is one of the most important differences between var and let in practice.
questions.concept: let creates a new binding per iteration
